THE CORE IDEA

runs.text: Monetary policy affects output by changing reserves and short-term interest rates, which influence investment, interest-sensitive consumption, and aggregate demand. Expansionary policy increases reserves and tends to lower interest rates, encouraging spending and shifting aggregate demand right. Contractionary policy works in the opposite direction. The strength of the transmission depends on bank lending, borrower response, and spending sensitivity to interest rates.

WORKED EXAMPLE: TRACING MONETARY TRANSMISSION

runs.text: Two panels show monetary-policy transmission. Left, interest rate r is vertical and money M horizontal. Money demand MD slopes downward. Vertical MS2 is left of MS1. Their intersections with MD are at the higher rate r2 for MS2 and lower rate r1 for MS1. Right, price level P is vertical and real output Y horizontal. Downward AD2 lies left of AD1. At the same marked price level P1, the point on AD2 is at Y2, left of Y1 on AD1. The contraction from MS1 to MS2 raises the interest rate and is paired with the leftward shift from AD1 to AD2; no numerical magnitudes are shown.

transcript.sourceText: In the money-market panel, contraction from MS1 to MS2 raises the interest rate from r1 to r2. Higher borrowing costs reduce interest-sensitive spending, so aggregate demand shifts from AD1 to AD2. At price level P1, real output demanded falls from Y1 to Y2. The panels display the complete monetary-policy transmission chain.
transcript.text: In the money-market panel, contraction from money supply one to money supply two raises the interest rate from interest rate r one to interest rate r two . Higher borrowing costs reduce interest-sensitive spending, so aggregate demand shifts from aggregate demand one to aggregate demand two . At price level price level P one , real output demanded falls from real output Y one to real output Y two . The panels display the complete monetary-policy transmission chain.
